title: Continuous Improvement Is Not About Perfection
summary: People often think continuous improvement is about finding the right solution and executing it flawlessly.
body_markdown:
**By Malte Hemmerich, Director Global Central Applications**


People often think continuous improvement is about finding the right solution and executing it flawlessly.


My experience has taught me something different. Continuous improvement is about learning.


Earlier this year, our Global Applications Engineering team faced a challenge familiar to many organizations. Growing demand along with competing priorities and expanding project scopes made it harder to align resources with the work that created the greatest value.


The issue was not effort. It was clarity.


During President’s Week, we launched a Kaizen focused on improving how we evaluate and prioritize application requests. Working with stakeholders across the business, we developed a new scoping process that helps define expectations and assess business value, aligning priorities before work begins.


The result was greater alignment and clearer communication, as well as more effective use of engineering resources. However, the most important lesson came after the Kaizen.


As we implemented the process, some improvements worked immediately while others revealed new challenges. Those moments reinforced that improvement does not end when a Kaizen event concludes. In many ways, that is when the real work begins.


Rather than assuming the first solution was enough, we continued gathering feedback and refining our approach. Progress rarely follows a straight line. It comes from testing ideas and learning from results, making adjustments along the way.


Mike Schnee, Sr. Director of Novanta Growth System, often describes continuous improvement as a cycle of learning and adjustment. When something is not working, the goal is not to repeat the same approach. It is to understand what has been learned and apply those insights moving forward.


This experience also reinforced the value of collaboration. Whitney Hedgpeth, Global Continuous Improvement Manager, brought perspectives from similar initiatives and helped us recognize that many challenges around communication, alignment, and visibility are shared across teams. Her insights helped us strengthen and refine our approach.


More importantly, those conversations demonstrated how much faster progress happens[when teams learn from one another](https://novanta.com/careers-culture/life-at-novanta/) . Fresh perspectives challenge assumptions and uncover blind spots while accelerating improvement.


Looking back, the biggest lesson was the importance of staying open to change. The willingness to reassess and improve ultimately produced a stronger outcome than simply staying the course.


[Markets evolve and customer needs change](https://novanta.com/about/vision-mission/) . New challenges constantly emerge. Continuous improvement is not about building a perfect process. It is about creating teams that are willing to learn and adapt.


For me, that is the true meaning of continuous improvement. Not perfection, but progress.
